title: The Afternoon Brief: Zverev, Alcaraz, and the US Open's fatigue test
dek: Friday's midday picture is shaped by two competing narratives at the US Open: defending and seeded players advancing through physical and mental ordeal, and the tournament's governance challenge over crowd conduct and spectator etiquette.
author: GoCheckMySports
key_fact: The US Open's bracket is being thinned by late-night finishes and mysterious medical episodes as much as by upsets, while the tournament grapples with how to manage a new class of credentialed influencers whose presence is dividing players on what tennis decorum should mean.
bottom_line: Friday's midday picture centers on how the US Open's bracket thins under both physical stress and crowd-conduct debate. Zverev and Alcaraz face the coming rounds after consecutive late finishes and injury return respectively, while Auger-Aliassime's unexplained medical episode opens a question the reporting does not resolve. The influencer etiquette divide among players, with Osaka and Pegula objecting, Gauff and Sabalenka supportive, remains unresolved by the USTA's existing crowd-management measures. The next checkpoint is Saturday's matches and the ongoing LSU-SEC eligibility ruling expected September 5.
body: The US Open is testing both the bodies and the authorities. Top seed Alexander Zverev finished his second-round match against Quentin Halys at 02:15 local time Friday after four hours and 33 minutes, marking his second five-set match in consecutive rounds and the first time any top seed in the Open era has played two five-setters in the first two rounds of a major. Third seed Felix Auger-Aliassime exited Thursday after reporting dizziness and vision disturbances he described as unprecedented in his career, losing to unseeded Karen Khachanov 6-7, 6-3, 6-2, 6-2. By contrast, Alcaraz, the defending champion returning from a four-month right wrist injury layoff, survived a first-set loss to Jaime Faria on Wednesday by winning eight consecutive games and advancing 4-6, 6-0, 6-3, 6-2. His progression against Faria showed control: Alcaraz fought off two break points in the opening game of the second set and reset his approach, sacrificing ambitious shotmaking for patience and longer rallies. The desk's league board shows Pegula holds 31 hard-court wins in 2026, breaking a tie with Rybakina for the most by any player on the women's tour, after her 56-minute dismissal of Sofia Kenin on Wednesday. Sabalenka, seeded first on the women's side, routed Polina Iatcenko 6-1, 6-1 in 53 minutes the same night, winning 15 of 16 first-serve points in the opening set.

The other narrative running through the tournament involves how tennis governs itself when crowds diversify. Around 100 credentialed content creators attended the 2026 US Open, and the presence has fractured the player consensus on what should be allowed. Osaka, the No. 13 seed, said after her third-round victory over Siniakova 6-2, 5-7, 6-1 on September 3 that an umpire had to address the crowd more than ever before, and she objected to the noise level and the behavior: "If you come to a sporting event, you have to respect the sport." Gauff, who defeated Badosa 6-4, 7-6 (5) on Thursday, took a different tone, saying she has no problem with influencers and that education about tennis etiquette, perhaps through signage in suites, might solve the problem: "If you're being invited to a red carpet, you wouldn't show up in jeans. I think it's just follow the etiquette of the sport." Pegula voiced frustration with ring lights and flash cameras during play, calling the practice "disrespectful." Sabalenka, by contrast, expressed support for influencer presence: "I love it, I love it. It's more eyes on our sport." Medvedev suggested chair umpires have sufficient tools to manage disturbances and that the issue occurs infrequently. The USTA has responded with reminders to ticket holders and video-board messaging but has not formalized new crowd rules. The gap between Pegula's and Sabalenka's views signals an unresolved question about how far commercial spectator engagement should extend during competition.

Elsewhere in the draw, Eala advanced to the third round by defeating Oleksandra Oliynykova 6-1, 6-4, with a No. 17 seeding and momentum from winning her first nine points. Navarro rallied past American Caty McNally 3-6, 6-2, 6-3 on Wednesday, her first win at the US Open after dropping a first set. Keys erased five match points against Bondar to win 5-7, 6-4, 7-6 (10-5). Swiatek and Anisimova won their second-round matches. On the men's side, the reporting does not offer a complete scoreboard update for all Friday matches, though Zverev's advance is confirmed.
